warmup.q: During a rolling deploy, 90% of your instances run v2, which adds a field to a JSON document. v1 instances decode the document into a data class that ignores unknown properties, update a status and write it back. A document gets 5 updates on random instances after the new field is set. Roughly what share of new-field values survive?
options: About 90%, the share of instances on v2
100%, because ignoring unknown properties keeps them
0%, because any v1 instance rejects the document
warmup.why: The value survives only if all 5 updates land on v2: 0.9^5 is about 0.59. Every update on v1 decodes into a class without the field and writes the class back, so one v1 touch erases it. "Ignore unknown properties" means "don't fail", not "keep them". Section 2 shows the mechanism and the fix.

sections.h: Data outlives code, and a deploy runs two versions at once
sections.html:
Your payouts table holds rows written last night and rows written in 2019. A deploy replaces the code in a few minutes, and it doesn't touch those rows. Every row stays in the shape and encoding it was written in until something rewrites it. Data outlives code. Writing a row is sending a message to your future self, who will be running different code.

So new code must read rows written by old code. That's backward compatibility from lesson 2, and in a database it isn't optional, because there is always old data.

Forward compatibility is needed too, because of the way you deploy. Your payout service runs as six instances behind a load balancer. A rolling upgrade replaces them one at a time: start a v2 instance, wait for its health check, stop a v1 instance, repeat. For those minutes some requests are served by v1 and some by v2, against the same tables, and a row v2 writes can be read by v1 a second later. A canary that runs at 5% for a day stretches that to a day. So do batch jobs and Kafka consumers still on last month's build, and so does a rollback, which is just a deploy in the other direction. You get a mixed-version fleet whether you plan for one or not.

Databases help by putting work off. In PostgreSQL, ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN with no default, or with a constant default, only changes the table's description in the system catalog. Old rows aren't touched; PostgreSQL fills in the default when it reads them. Since PostgreSQL 11 that holds even for NOT NULL DEFAULT 'EUR'. A volatile default such as clock_timestamp() is different: every row needs its own value, so PostgreSQL rewrites the whole table and its indexes into a new file while holding an exclusive lock. The Try-it shows both on a million rows.

What the database can't do for you is change what data means. Turning euros into cents, splitting one field into two, or moving data into its own table means rewriting rows while code that expects the old shape is still running. The rest of this lesson is about doing that without breaking either version. Keep this picture: a timeline of code versions that overlap in pairs, over data that spans all of them.

try.title: Add a column to a million rows, twice
steps: From the labs folder, start PostgreSQL 18 with docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait and open a prompt with docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz.
Create a million-row payouts table and note its file number, then add a column with a constant default (block below).
Predict before the last ALTER: will a clock_timestamp() default change the file number? How long will it take compared with the first ALTER?
Keep the prompt and the table: the Try-its in sections 3 and 4 use them.

code.title: psql, database sfz
code.html: CREATE TABLE payouts AS SELECT g AS id, 'merchant-' || (g % 50) AS merchant, (g * 7 / 100.0)::numeric(12,2) AS amount FROM generate_series(1, 1000000) g; SELECT pg_relation_filenode('payouts') AS file, pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('payouts')) AS size; \timing on ALTER TABLE payouts ADD COLUMN currency text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'EUR'; SELECT pg_relation_filenode('payouts') AS file; SELECT id, amount, currency FROM payouts WHERE id = 1; ALTER TABLE payouts ADD COLUMN created_at timestamptz DEFAULT clock_timestamp(); SELECT pg_relation_filenode('payouts') AS file, pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('payouts')) AS size;

try.expect:
file  | size
-------+-------
 16385 | 56 MB

ALTER TABLE
Time: 1.336 ms
 file
-------
 16385

 id | amount | currency
----+--------+----------
  1 |   0.07 | EUR

ALTER TABLE
Time: 731.523 ms

-------+-------

(blank lines and row counts trimmed; your file numbers and times will differ). The constant default took about a millisecond and left the same file: the million old rows weren't touched, and PostgreSQL fills in EUR when it reads them. The clock_timestamp() default rewrote every row into a new, bigger file, holding an exclusive lock the whole time. On a 50 GB table that's minutes of blocked traffic.

sections.h: Old code that writes a record back deletes what it doesn't know
sections.html:
Here is the most common way a mixed fleet loses data. A customer document lives in a jsonb column. v2 adds preferredLanguage and a settings screen to set it. v1 has never heard of it, and handles a status update like this:

data class CustomerV1(val id: Int, val name: String, val status: String)

fun updateStatus(stored: String, status: String): String {
    val c: CustomerV1 = mapper.readValue(stored)        // preferredLanguage has nowhere to go
    return mapper.writeValueAsString(c.copy(status = status))
}

Plain Jackson fails on a property the class doesn't have, which would at least be loud. But Quarkus and Spring Boot both configure their ObjectMapper to ignore unknown properties. So the decode succeeds, the language is dropped, and the encode writes a document without it. Nothing logs anything. The stepper below walks through it.

How much is lost? Say a customer sets a language (on v2, the only version with that screen) and then gets five status updates, each landing on a random instance. The language survives only if all five land on v2. With 90% of the fleet on v2, that's 0.9^5, about 59%, so 41% of the languages set during the rollout are gone. At 50% it's 97%. The Try-it simulates exactly this, and so does the lab.

The fix is to change only what you own. Read the document as a tree (ObjectNode), set status and write the tree back, so properties you don't know ride along. Or don't read and write the whole document at all: UPDATE customers SET doc = jsonb_set(doc, '{status}', '"active"') WHERE id = ? changes one key inside the database. Protobuf does the first for you, since protobuf-java keeps unknown fields and writes them back (lesson 2). Avro doesn't: decode with v1's reader's schema, encode with it again, and the new field is gone.

The same trap appears without JSON columns. A cache that stores whole v1 objects, and a consumer that reads an event, adds something and republishes it, both drop new fields the same way. An ORM is mostly safe for a new column it doesn't map, because its UPDATE never mentions that column, but a v1 INSERT leaves it NULL, which the next section's migration has to handle.

try.title: Measure the loss against the rollout percentage
steps: Open RolloutDemo.kt. 1,000 customers each set a language on v2, then get 5 status updates on random instances. v1 runs either the data-class code or the tree code.
Predict the data-class loss at 50%, 90% and 99% v2 before you run it.

code.title: RolloutDemo.kt (the two v1 versions)
code.html: /** v1 the usual way: decode into the data class, change it, encode it. */ fun dataClassTouch(stored: String, status: String): String = mapper.writeValueAsString(mapper.readValue<CustomerV1>(stored).copy(status = status)) /** v1 the careful way: change one property of the tree, keep the rest. */ fun treeTouch(stored: String, status: String): String = mapper.writeValueAsString((mapper.readTree(stored) as ObjectNode).put("status", status))

v2 share   lost, data class   lost, tree   1 - p^5
     10%              100.0%          0.0%    100.0%
     50%               96.5%          0.0%     96.9%
     90%               41.2%          0.0%     41.0%
     99%                4.9%          0.0%      4.9%
    100%                0.0%          0.0%      0.0%

The simulation lands on the formula: a value survives only if every later update hits v2. Even at 99% upgraded, about one language in twenty is erased. With the tree code, nothing is lost at any percentage.

sections.h: Knight Capital: one server on old code, one flag with a new meaning
sections.html:
On 1 August 2012, Knight Capital, a large US market maker, lost more than $460 million in about 45 minutes. The SEC's 2013 order lays out how, and the cause is a mixed-version fleet.

Knight's order router, SMARS, ran on eight servers. For a new NYSE program, the Retail Liquidity Program (RLP), developers wrote new code and repurposed a flag that had once switched on an old feature called Power Peg. Knight had stopped using Power Peg in 2003, but its code was still in the router and could still be called. In 2005 someone moved the part of the router that counted how many shares of an order had been filled, and nobody retested Power Peg afterwards. Starting on 27 July, Knight deployed the RLP code in stages over several days. A technician didn't copy it to one of the eight servers, and no second person reviewed the deployment.

On 1 August, orders arrived with the flag set. Seven servers ran the new RLP code correctly. The eighth ran Power Peg, which, with its fill counter gone, kept sending child orders without ever noticing the parent order was filled. For 212 customer orders it sent millions of orders: 4 million executions in 154 stocks, more than 397 million shares, leaving Knight about $3.5 billion long and $3.15 billion short. While trying to fix it, the team removed the new code from the seven good servers. The flag still arrived, Power Peg was still there, and now all eight servers ran it. Earlier that morning, 97 automated emails had reported "Power Peg disabled" before the market opened; they weren't designed as alerts, and staff generally didn't read them. The SEC fined Knight $12 million.

Take away the trading and three lessons are left:

  • A staged deploy is a mixed-version fleet. One server out of eight was a 12.5% rollout that nobody knew about, and the rollback was another deploy that made it 100%.
  • Repurposing an identifier is reusing a Protobuf field number (lesson 2). The bits stay the same, the meaning changes, and old code acts on the old meaning without an error. Flags, enum values, status codes and columns all count.
  • Dead code that can still run is part of your compatibility surface. Delete it, and let a full release go by before anything reuses what it used.

The database version of the flag is changing what a column means in place. ALTER TABLE refunds ALTER COLUMN amount TYPE bigint USING (amount * 100)::bigint turns euros into cents in one statement. Every v1 instance still running keeps inserting 40.00, meaning forty euros, and PostgreSQL stores it in the new column as 40, which now means forty cents. Nobody gets an error.

try.title: Change a column's meaning in place, then watch v1 write
steps: In the psql prompt from section 1, run the block below. The ALTER is v2's migration; the second INSERT is a v1 instance that hasn't been replaced yet.
Predict the two amounts before you look.

code.title: psql, database sfz
code.html: CREATE TABLE refunds (id bigint PRIMARY KEY, amount numeric(12,2) NOT NULL); INSERT INTO refunds VALUES (1, 40.00); -- v2's migration: the same column now holds cents ALTER TABLE refunds ALTER COLUMN amount TYPE bigint USING (amount * 100)::bigint; -- a v1 instance that hasn't been replaced yet inserts 40.00 euros, as it always has INSERT INTO refunds VALUES (2, 40.00); SELECT * FROM refunds ORDER BY id;

try.expect:
id | amount
----+--------
  1 |   4000
  2 |     40

Both refunds were 40 euros. Row 2 now reads as 40 cents, and every statement succeeded: PostgreSQL rounds a numeric into a bigint column without complaint. The fix is never to change a column's meaning in place. Add amount_minor next to it, as in section 4.

sections.h: Change the schema in phases: expand, migrate, contract
sections.html:
Back to payouts. The amount column holds euros as numeric(12,2), and you want amount_minor, a bigint of cents, like every other money field in the company. The quick way is one migration that renames and converts the column, shipped with the deploy. The lab tries it: the moment it runs, every v1 instance still in the fleet fails with column "amount" does not exist (SQLSTATE 42703) until the rollout finishes. Stopping the service first avoids the errors, but the downtime grows with the table. Stripe worked out that migrating 100 million records at one per second would take more than three years.

What works is expand and contract, also called parallel change. First expand the schema so it supports the old and the new shape at once. Then move readers and writers across, one rollout at a time. Then contract the schema to the new shape. Stripe's version, from its 2017 post about moving hundreds of millions of subscriptions into their own table, has four phases: dual-write, switch reads, switch writes, remove the old data. For payouts it takes six steps:

  1. Expand: ALTER TABLE payouts ADD COLUMN amount_minor bigint. It's nullable with no default, so it only changes the catalog, and v1's inserts, which don't mention it, keep working.
  2. Deploy v2, which writes both columns in one statement and still reads amount. While v1 and v2 overlap, a v1 instance can change amount on a row v2 just wrote, which leaves amount_minor stale.
  3. Backfill, after the last v1 instance is gone: copy round(amount * 100) into amount_minor wherever it is NULL or different, in batches of a few thousand rows, each its own short transaction, so locks and WAL stay small.
  4. Deploy v3, which reads amount_minor. Stripe used GitHub's Scientist library to run the old and the new read side by side and log every difference. The lab's v3 counts mismatches the same way.
  5. Let amount be NULL and make amount_minor NOT NULL, then deploy v4, which writes only amount_minor. PostgreSQL 18 can add that NOT NULL as NOT VALID and check the existing rows later with VALIDATE CONSTRAINT, which takes a weaker lock that lets reads and writes go on.
  6. Contract: once no running version mentions amount, drop it.

Every step works with the code versions on both sides of it. That's the whole trick, and the figure shows it. Each schema step is its own Flyway migration (the SQL track's lesson on SQL from the JVM), so a change that used to be one file becomes a process that takes several deploys and maybe weeks.

One hazard remains. Every ALTER TABLE above except VALIDATE takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, even the instant ones. If any open transaction holds a lock on the table, the ALTER waits for it, and every query that arrives after the ALTER queues behind it. A one-millisecond ALTER behind a forgotten BEGIN stops all reads of the table. Set lock_timeout to a few seconds before DDL on a busy table, and retry when it fails.

figure.caption: Two columns live side by side from phase 1 to phase 5. Each rollout overlaps only two versions, and each schema step works with both.

try.title: Watch an instant ALTER block every read
steps: Open three psql prompts on the same database (docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz), called A, B and C below.
In A, start a transaction that reads payouts and leave it open: BEGIN; SELECT count(*) FROM payouts;
In B, run ALTER TABLE payouts ADD COLUMN amount_minor bigint;. In C, run SELECT amount FROM payouts WHERE id = 42;. Both hang.
In a fourth prompt, or in A, look at who waits (query below). Then COMMIT; in A and watch B and C finish.

Repeat with a timeout: start A's transaction again, and in B run SET lock_timeout = '2s'; before ALTER TABLE payouts ADD COLUMN fee_minor bigint;. Then COMMIT; in A. When you're done, DROP TABLE payouts, refunds; and stop the database with docker compose -f env/postgres.yml down.

code.title: who is waiting for whom
code.html: SELECT pid, state, wait_event_type AS wait, left(query, 50) AS query FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE datname = 'sfz' AND pid <> pg_backend_pid() ORDER BY backend_start;

try.expect:
pid |        state        |  wait  |                       query
-----+---------------------+--------+----------------------------------------------------
 191 | idle in transaction | Client | SELECT count(*) FROM payouts;
 200 | active              | Lock   | ALTER TABLE payouts ADD COLUMN amount_minor2 bigin
 207 | active              | Lock   | SELECT amount FROM payouts WHERE id = 42

(captured with a slightly different column name; your pids differ). A holds a lock that lets others read, B wants an exclusive one and waits, and C's plain read waits behind B, because PostgreSQL queues lock requests in order. With the timeout, B gives up instead and C never waits:

ERROR:  canceling statement due to lock timeout
Time: 2001.270 ms (00:02.001)

video.title: Expand and contract: changing a column under live traffic

analogy: Expand and contract is how a city replaces a bridge. It builds the new bridge next to the old one (expand), opens it while the old one still carries traffic, moves the bus routes over one at a time (dual write, switch reads, switch writes), and only demolishes the old bridge (contract) once no route uses it. Renaming in place is closing the old bridge on Monday and hoping every driver read the notice. The analogy breaks on the backfill: cars don't need to be copied from one bridge to the other, while every old row has to be moved across, in batches, while traffic keeps writing new ones.
world: Your Quarkus payment services deploy as rolling updates on Kubernetes, so every release runs two versions side by side for a few minutes, and Temporal workers on the old build keep processing workflows until they drain. Treat every schema change as two-sided: can the old pods live with the new schema, and can the new pods read rows the old ones keep writing? Oracle adds a nullable column instantly too, and since Oracle 11g a NOT NULL column with a default is a metadata change as well, but Oracle commits DDL immediately, so a failed multi-step migration leaves you halfway. For money columns, never change units in place: add amount_minor, dual-write, backfill, switch, and drop the old column a release later. And look for any flag, status code or enum value someone plans to "reuse": that's Knight's bug waiting for a deploy.
mistake: Shipping the contract step with the change that makes it possible. A team moves reads and writes to amount_minor in v4 and puts ALTER TABLE payouts DROP COLUMN amount in the same release's Flyway migration. Flyway runs it when the first v4 pod starts, while the other pods are still v3 and still write amount, so every v3 write fails with SQLSTATE 42703 until the rollout ends, and a rollback to v3 is now impossible because the column is gone. People do it because the migration and the code "belong together". The fix is to ship each contract step one release after the code stopped using the old column, and to keep rollback possible: a release must work with the schema of the release before it.

compare.title: Renaming a column in one step, and in phases

a.label: In one step
a.title: V3__amount_in_cents.sql
a.html: -- runs when the first v2 pod starts ALTER TABLE payouts RENAME COLUMN amount TO amount_minor; ALTER TABLE payouts ALTER COLUMN amount_minor TYPE bigint USING (amount_minor * 100)::bigint; -- rewrites the table -- every v1 pod still running: -- ERROR: column "amount" does not exist (42703)

b.label: In phases
b.title: one migration per release
b.html: -- release 2: expand (instant), code dual-writes ALTER TABLE payouts ADD COLUMN amount_minor bigint; -- between releases: batched backfill job -- release 3: code reads amount_minor -- release 4: code writes only amount_minor ALTER TABLE payouts ALTER COLUMN amount DROP NOT NULL; ALTER TABLE payouts ADD CONSTRAINT payouts_amount_minor_not_null NOT NULL amount_minor NOT VALID; -- release 5: contract ALTER TABLE payouts DROP COLUMN amount;

compare.note: The one-step version is shorter, takes an exclusive lock for a full table rewrite, breaks every old pod at once and can't be rolled back. The phased version never has a moment where a running version and the schema disagree, and every step is quick, except the backfill, which runs in small transactions while traffic continues.

worked.title: Write the payouts migration as Flyway files and a backfill job

steps.say: Release 2 ships the expand migration with the dual-writing code. SET LOCAL scopes the timeout to the migration's own transaction, so a long transaction on payouts makes the deploy fail and retry instead of freezing the table.
steps.code: -- V3__payouts_expand.sql (subgoal: add the new column without blocking anyone for long) SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '5s'; ALTER TABLE payouts ADD COLUMN amount_minor bigint;

steps.say: The backfill is a job, not a migration: it may run for hours, and it must be safe to stop and restart. It starts only after the last v1 pod is gone. Each batch is its own transaction, and the WHERE clause finds the remaining work, so a restart just continues.
steps.code: // subgoal: copy old to new in small, restartable batches fun backfill(conn: Connection, batch: Int = 5_000) { var total = 0 while (true) { val n = Migration.backfillBatch(conn, batch) // UPDATE ... WHERE id IN (... LIMIT ?) if (n == 0) break total += n log.info("backfilled $total payouts") Thread.sleep(50) // leave room for live traffic and replication } }

steps.say: Release 4 switches writes. Split the constraint into two migrations: Flyway runs each file in one transaction, and the ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock from ADD CONSTRAINT would otherwise be held for the whole validation scan.
steps.code: -- V5__payouts_switch_writes.sql (subgoal: old column optional, new one required for new rows) SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '5s'; ALTER TABLE payouts ALTER COLUMN amount DROP NOT NULL; ALTER TABLE payouts ADD CONSTRAINT payouts_amount_minor_not_null NOT NULL amount_minor NOT VALID; -- V6__payouts_validate.sql (subgoal: check old rows under a lock that allows reads and writes) ALTER TABLE payouts VALIDATE CONSTRAINT payouts_amount_minor_not_null;

steps.say: Release 5, at least one release after v4 is everywhere, contracts. By then no running version, and no version you might roll back to, mentions amount.
steps.code: -- V7__payouts_contract.sql (subgoal: remove the old shape once nothing can use it) SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '5s'; ALTER TABLE payouts DROP COLUMN amount;

lab.title: Measure field loss in a rolling upgrade, then migrate a live table with expand and contract
steps: Run the tests once from the labs folder. All 12 fail. The first run pulls postgres:18 if you don't have it; after that the container starts in a few seconds.
In FieldLoss.kt, write PreservingCodec: read the JSON as an ObjectNode, put the new status, write it back.

Write RollingUpgrade.lossRate: create the documents, set every language through V2, then send each customer's updates to v2 or v1 with Random(seed), and count the documents without a language. The six FieldLossTest tests should pass now, including the 1 - p^5 curve.

In Payouts.kt, write Migration.expand, PayoutsV2.save (one upsert that writes both columns), Migration.backfillBatch and Migration.contract. PayoutsV1, PayoutsV3, PayoutsV4 and prepareSwitchWrites are complete; read them first.

Run the tests until all 12 pass. ExpandContractTest runs each rollout as 400 interleaved requests on two versions, and checks for zero errors and zero wrong reads, and that a too-early backfill or contract does break things.
hints: mapper.readTree(stored) as ObjectNode gives you a mutable tree; put("status", newStatus) returns the same node.
Route each update with if (rnd.nextInt(100) < v2Percent) V2.touch(doc, "active") else v1.touch(doc, "active"), and make all Random calls in the same order every run, or the seed won't repeat.

The backfill must also fix rows where amount_minor is set but wrong: a v1 instance can change amount after v2 wrote both. amount_minor IS DISTINCT FROM round(amount * 100)::bigint is true for NULL and for wrong values.
If only ExpandContractTest fails with a Docker error, start Docker Desktop. FieldLossTest needs no Docker.

drill.title: Plan a column rename from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lesson. The customers table must rename email to email_address, with six instances running and no downtime. Write the steps in order: for each, the SQL (if any) and which code versions run during it. Then check: when does the backfill run, and when is email dropped?

answer.html:
1. Expand:   ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN email_address text;     -- v1 runs, unaffected
2. Deploy v2: writes email AND email_address, reads email           -- v1 + v2 overlap
3. Backfill:  UPDATE ... SET email_address = email
              WHERE email_address IS DISTINCT FROM email (batches)  -- only v2 runs
4. Deploy v3: reads email_address, still writes both               -- v2 + v3 overlap
5. ALTER email DROP NOT NULL; email_address NOT NULL (NOT VALID, then VALIDATE)
   Deploy v4: writes only email_address                             -- v3 + v4 overlap
6. One release later: ALTER TABLE customers DROP COLUMN email;      -- only v4 runs
Every ALTER: SET lock_timeout first.

recap: Data outlives code: rows keep the shape they were written in, so new code must read old data (backward compatibility).
A rolling upgrade, a canary or a rollback runs two versions at once, so old code also reads data written by new code (forward compatibility).

Old code that decodes into its own class and writes the class back deletes fields it doesn't know. With 5 later updates, a field survives a rollout at p% only with probability p^5. Change only what you own.
Knight Capital lost over $460 million when one of eight servers kept old code and a repurposed flag switched it on. Never give an old identifier a new meaning.
Expand and contract changes a schema in steps that each work with the versions on both sides: add, dual-write, backfill, switch reads, switch writes, drop. Set lock_timeout before DDL.

explain.prompt: A colleague wants to change payouts.amount from euros to cents with one ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE bigint USING amount * 100 in the next release's migration. Explain what goes wrong during the rolling deploy and what you'd do instead.
explain.answer: The migration runs when the first new pod starts, but the old pods keep running for a while and keep writing euros into the same column: 40.00 becomes 40, which the new code reads as 40 cents. Nothing errors, so nobody notices until reconciliation. The ALTER also rewrites the whole table under an exclusive lock, and a rollback can't undo the meaning change. Instead I'd expand and contract: add a nullable amount_minor (instant), ship code that writes both columns, backfill amount_minor in batches once no old pod is left, ship code that reads amount_minor with a shadow comparison, then code that writes only amount_minor, and drop amount a release later. Every step works with the versions on either side, and each ALTER gets a lock_timeout.

deeper.html:
Designing Data-Intensive Applications (2nd edition, chapter 5) describes the database as a message to your future self and calls keeping compatibility across complex migrations an open research problem. Project Cambria (Ink & Switch, 2020) is one research answer: "lenses" that translate each record between schema versions on read and write, so old and new code each see their own shape.

Tools now automate parts of expand and contract on PostgreSQL. pgroll, for example, puts a schema of views over the real tables for each version, backfills a new column from the old one, and keeps the two in sync with triggers until the migration completes, so old and new code each pick their version through search_path. For MySQL, gh-ost and pt-online-schema-change copy the table in the background and switch over at the end. They solve the locking and the copying. They don't solve meaning: deciding that amount is euros and amount_minor is cents, and that no flag is ever reused, is still your job.

Stripe's post is worth reading in full for the parts this lesson skipped: how they used Hadoop jobs over database snapshots to find the records to migrate, and how they compared millions of reads with Scientist before trusting the new path.
